content: Optical brighteners, also known as optical brightening agents (OBAs), fluorescent brightening agents (FBAs), or fluorescent whitening agents (FWAs), are chemical dyes that absorb light in the ultraviolet (UV) and violet regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, typically between 340 and 370 nanometers. These compounds then re-emit the absorbed energy as light in the blue region of the visible spectrum, usually between 420 and 470 nanometers. The fluorescence exhibited by these agents is a rapid emission of light, distinct from phosphorescence, which involves a delayed emission. Optical brighteners are commonly added to materials such as fabrics and paper to enhance their visual appearance. By increasing the amount of blue light reflected, they create a whitening effect, which reduces the perception of yellow tones and makes the treated materials appear brighter and whiter. The most prevalent class of chemicals used as optical brighteners includes stilbenes and fluorescent dyes like umbelliferone. These compounds absorb UV light and re-emit it in the blue portion of the visible spectrum. When applied to a white surface, optical brighteners increase the amount of visible light emitted, making the surface appear brighter than it would under normal lighting conditions. The blue light emitted by these agents effectively masks yellow and brown tones, further enhancing the whiteness of the treated material. There are approximately 400 types of optical brighteners listed in the Color Index, but fewer than 90 are produced commercially, and only a small subset holds significant commercial importance. Each fluorescent brightening agent can be assigned a specific identification number, although some numbers are duplicated due to manufacturers applying for the same index number when producing the compound. Global production of optical brighteners for use in paper, textiles, and detergents is dominated by a few specific chemical types, such as diand tetra-sulfonated triazole-stilbenes and di-sulfonated stilbene-biphenyl compounds. However, these compounds are prone to degradation when exposed to prolonged UV light. This degradation occurs due to the formation of optically inactive cis-isomers of stilbene at the molecular center. All optical brighteners share a common feature of extended conjugation and/or aromaticity, which facilitates electron movement within the molecule. Non-stilbene optical brighteners are sometimes used in more permanent applications, such as whitening synthetic fibers. The basic classes of optical brighteners can be enhanced (boosted) by the addition of certain polyols, such as high molecular weight polyethylene glycol or polyvinyl alcohol, which significantly increase the visible blue light emissions. Conversely, excessive use of optical brighteners can lead to a quenching effect, where the material takes on a greenish hue as emissions extend beyond the blue region of the visible spectrum. In stilbene-based brighteners, only the trans-isomer is optically active. Prolonged exposure to UV light not only promotes the formation of inactive cis-isomers but can also cleave the molecule, initiating its degradation. Optical brighteners are frequently added to laundry detergents to replace whitening agents lost during washing and to make clothes appear cleaner. These agents have largely replaced the older practice of bluing, which was used to achieve a similar whitening effect. Some optical brighteners can cause allergic reactions when they come into contact with the skin. They are also widely used in the production of high-brightness papers, giving these papers a strongly fluorescent appearance under UV illumination. The brightness of paper is typically measured at 457 nanometers, which falls within the fluorescent activity range of optical brighteners. Notably, paper used for banknotes does not contain optical brighteners, making fluorescence testing a common method for detecting counterfeit notes. Special care must be taken to avoid washing military uniforms, such as the Army Combat Uniform (ACU) and Marine Corps Combat Utility Uniform (MCCUU), with detergents containing optical brighteners. These agents can make the uniforms more visible under night vision devices or in low-light conditions, potentially compromising the wearer's concealment.
